sections.title: 英语知识运用
sections.directions: Directions: Read the following text. Choose the best word(s) for each numbered blank and mark A, B, C or D on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

blocks.content: Comparisons were drawn between the development of television in the 20th century and the diffusion of printing in the 15th and 16th centuries. Yet much had happened
. As was discussed before, it was not
the 19th century that the newspaper became the dominant pre-electronic
, following in the wake of the pamphlet and the book and in the
of the periodical. It was during the same time that the communications revolution
up, beginning with transport, the railway, and leading
through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures
the 20th century world of the motor car and the airplane. Not everyone sees that process in
. It is important to do so. It is generally recognized,
, that the introduction of the computer in the early 20th century,
by the invention of the integrated circuit during the 1960s, radically changed the process,
its impact on the media was not immediately
. As time went by, computers became smaller and more powerful, and they became "personal" too, as well as
, with display becoming sharper and storage
increasing. They were thought of, like people,
generations, with the distance between generations much
. It was within the computer age that the term "information society" began to be widely used to describe the
within which we now live. The communications revolution has
both work and leisure and how we think and feel both about place and time, but there have been
views about its economic, political, social and cultural implications. "Benefits" have been weighed
"harmful" outcomes. And generalizations have proved difficult.

questions.analysis: between 【线索】锚定两个相隔几百年的时间点 前句给出两个端点——20 世纪的电视与 15-16 世纪的印刷（the development of television in the 20th century and the diffusion of printing in the 15th and 16th centuries），而过去完成时 had happened 强调「在对照之前的这段跨度里」许多事已发 【选项】 A) between ✓ 两端点之间，正契合 时 had happened 表达「这段区间里发生了很多」完全吻合。 B) before ✗ 无明确终点参照 C) since ✗ 只起点不闭合 D) later ✗ 晚于某点不切题 【验证】代入后：Yet much had happened between. 与前句两个时间点形成自然呼应，与全文

until 【线索】强调句框架 it was not ... that ... 本句为强调句 it was not __(2)__ the 19th century that the newspaper became the dominant pre-electronic __(3)__，要被强调的是「直到 19 世纪报纸才成为主导前电子媒 【选项】A) after ✗ 破坏 not until 句式 after 与 not 连用只能表「不在……之后」，不能构成「直到 19 世纪才……」的强调含义。 B) by ✗ 时态不匹配 C) during ✗ 无 not during 强调句 D) until ✓ not until 强调句完美契合 until 与 it was not...that 共同构成 it was not until + 时间 + that 句型，意为「直到 19 世纪报 纸才成为主导的前电子媒介」，与紧随其后的「following in the wake of the pamphlet and the book」时间线吻合。 【验证】代入后：it was not until the 19th century that the newspaper became the dominant

medium 【线索】「报纸」是传播信息的载体 the newspaper became the dominant pre-electronic __(3)__, following in the wake of the pamphlet and the book：报纸、小册子、书都是传播信息的载体（媒介），且修饰语 pre-electronic（前电子的）正与「电子媒介」对应。 【选项】A) means ✗ 义近但层级不对 means 表「手段、方法」，可说 means of communication（交流手段），但 pre-electronic medium 是固定表「前电子时代媒介」的术语，means 不与 pre-electronic 搭配。 B) method ✗ 侧重方法步骤 method 指做事的「方法、步骤」，与报纸作为传播载体的身份对不上，也无 pre-electronic method 的惯用搭配。 C) medium ✓ 传播媒介，精准对位 medium 即「媒介、媒体」，pre-electronic medium 意为「前电子时代的媒介」，与报纸、小 册子、书的并列身份完全吻合，且承接全文「communications revolution」的话题术语。 D) measure ✗ 措施义不沾边 【验证】代入后：the newspaper became the dominant pre-electronic medium，报纸作为「主 导前电子媒介」的定性自然，且与下文 motion pictures、radio 等电子媒介形成历史对

company 【线索】与 in the wake of 形成并列 following in the wake of the pamphlet and the book and in the __(4)__ of the periodical：「紧随小册子和书之后，并和期刊__一起__」，这里 and 连接两个介词短语， 【选项】A) process ✗ 无 in the process of the X 这种用法 process 与 of 搭配通常是 in the process of doing sth（正在做……的过程中），后接动名词而非 名词，与 the periodical 这一具体载体名词搭配不当。 B) company ✓ in the company of 与 ... 一起 company 与 in the ___ of 构成 in the company of「与……为伴／一起」，呼应前半 following C) light ✗ in the light of 是「鉴于」 light 与 of 搭配成 in the light of「鉴于、根据」，引出依据或缘由，但报纸不是「鉴于期刊」才 D) form ✗ in the form of 是「以……的形式」 form 与 of 搭配成 in the form of「以……的形式」，但报纸并不「以期刊的形式」存在——它本 【验证】代入后：following in the wake of the pamphlet and the book and in the company of

speeded 【线索】革命要「加速发展」 It was during the same time that the communications revolution __(5)__ up, beginning with transport, the railway, and leading __(6)__ through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures：随后列举一连串发明，呈现的是节奏越来越快的 【选项】A) gathered ✗ gather up 是「收拢」 B) speeded ✓ speed up 加速，与下文连续发明吻合 C) worked ✗ work up 表激起情绪 D) picked ✗ pick up 偏「拾起／回暖」 【验证】代入后：the communications revolution speeded up, beginning with transport, the railway, and leading __(6)__ through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion

on 【线索】下文 through ... into 描绘连续推进 leading __(6)__ through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures __(7)__ the 20th century world of the motor car and the airplane：through 串起多项 【选项】 A) on ✓ lead on 继续向前推进 on 与 lead 构成 lead on「继续向前」，且与下文 through ... into 的递进路径完美呼应，整体 时代」。 B) out ✗ lead out 表「带出」 C) over ✗ lead over 不是固定方向词 D) off ✗ lead off 表「带头开始」 off 与 lead 构成 lead off「带头、开始」，但句中「beginning with transport」已明示起点，此 【验证】代入后：leading on through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures __(7)__ the 20th century world of the motor car and the airplane，「持续向

into 【线索】lead on through ... 终点在「20 世纪世界」 本句承上 leading __(6)__ through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures __(7)__ the 20th century world of the motor car and the airplane：lead on 【选项】A) of ✗ of 表所属，方向丢失 B) for ✗ for 表目的或对象 for 表「为了、对……来说」，无法承接「lead on through」的推进路径，逻辑断裂。 C) beyond ✗ beyond 越出范围相反 D) into ✓ into 表「进入新时代」 into 表「进入」，与前文 lead on through 串起的推进路径完美收束：贯穿电报、电话、广播、 【验证】代入后：leading on through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures into the 20th century world of the motor car and the airplane，「继续向前

perspective 【线索】本段宏大的「过程」需被通盘审视 前文 beginning with transport, the railway, and leading on through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures into the 20th century world of the motor car and the airplane 描绘了一个跨数百年的宏大进程，作者随即评论 Not everyone sees that process in __(8)__. It is important to do so. 表示要从整体视角看待这一进程。 【选项】A) concept ✗ 概念义不切 concept 意为「概念」，see ... in concept 不是惯用搭配，且语义指向是「以概念形式看」，与 B) dimension ✗ 维度不指整体视角 dimension 表「维度、方面」，see sth in dimension 不是固定搭配，也无法表达「整体审视」的 C) effect ✗ in effect 是「实际上」 effect 与 in 搭配是 in effect「实际上、生效」，意思与「看待过程的视角」对不上，逻辑跳脱。 D) perspective ✓ in perspective 整体视角，精准对位 perspective 与 in 构成 see ... in perspective「以恰当/整体的视角看」，与下文 It is important to do so. 强调「应当这么看」遥相呼应，是地道写法。 【验证】代入后：Not everyone sees that process in perspective. It is important to do so.，

however 【线索】由「并非人人都从整体视角看」转入「但人们普遍承认……」 上段末 Not everyone sees that process in __(8)__. It is important to do so. 暗含「很多 人没意识到这一点」；本段开头 It is generally recognized, __(9)__, that the introduction of the computer...radically changed the process 却说「人们普遍承认计算机的引入彻底 【选项】A) indeed ✗ 递进强调，方向不对 B) hence ✗ 因果，没有因 C) however ✓ however 转折，精准对位 D) therefore ✗ 因果，错向 【验证】代入后：It is generally recognized, however, that the introduction of the computer in the early 20th century...radically changed the process，「然而，人们普遍承认……」的

followed 【线索】计算机引入「在 20 世纪初」，集成电路发明「在 1960 年代」 本句给了两个时间锚点：the introduction of the computer in the early 20th century 在 前，the invention of the integrated circuit during the 1960s 在后，是「先有计算机引 【选项】A) brought ✗ 需要 about/in 才能成搭配 brought 多与 about/in/on 搭配（bring about=带来），单独 brought by sth 一般指「被某人 B) followed ✓ followed by 后续接力，时序对位 followed 与 by 构成「X followed by Y」=X 之后是 Y。计算机引入在 20 世纪初，集成电路在 C) stimulated ✗ 因果反向 stimulated by Y 意思是「被 Y 所刺激/推动」，则要求 Y 在 X 之前并推动 X，但事实是 Y（集成 D) characterized ✗ characterized by 表特征 characterized by Y 表「以 Y 为特征」，但 Y 是后来的发明，不能成为 X（计算机引入）的特征， 【验证】代入后：the introduction of the computer in the early 20th century, followed by the invention of the integrated circuit during the 1960s, radically changed the process，

although 【线索】「彻底改变」VS「冲击并非立即显现」 主句 radically changed the process 是肯定影响，从句 its impact on the media was not immediately __(12)__ 表达「冲击并未立即显现」——一个强一个弱，构成让步对比 【选项】A) unless ✗ 条件假设，不切 B) since ✗ 因果方向反 C) lest ✗ lest 表「以免」 D) although ✓ although 让步，精准对位 【验证】代入后：radically changed the process, although its impact on the media was not

apparent 【线索】下文随时间逐步显化 紧随其后：As time went by, computers became smaller and more powerful, and they became "personal" too：随着时间推移，计算机才慢慢变小变强、变得个人化——意味着 【选项】 A) apparent ✓ apparent 明显，与下文「随时间显化」吻合 apparent 表「明显的」，not immediately apparent = 不是立即明显的，恰好对应下文 As time went by, computers became smaller and more powerful 「随时间逐步显化」的过程。 B) desirable ✗ 色彩偏好不切 C) negative ✗ 无负面定性铺垫 D) plausible ✗ 似乎合理偏推断 【验证】代入后：its impact on the media was not immediately apparent，「冲击并未立即

institutional 【线索】与「个人化」形成场景对照 they became "personal" too, as well as __(13)__：personal 用了引号特意点明「个人使 【选项】 A) institutional ✓ 与 personal 完美对位 institutional 表「机构的」，与 personal「个人的」构成「使用主体」轴上的并列对照——计 B) universal ✗ 普遍化偏程度 universal 表「普遍的、通用的」，描述的是「普及程度」而非「使用主体」，与 personal 不是同 C) fundamental ✗ 「基础的」与并列轴无关 fundamental 表「基础的、根本的」，描述重要性，与 personal 这一「使用场景」标签不在同一 D) instrumental ✗ 「起作用的」与场景轴不符 instrumental 表「起作用的、有助益的」，强调功能贡献，与 personal 的对照面对不上。 【验证】代入后：they became "personal" too, as well as institutional，「既个人化也机构化」

capacity 【线索】storage 谈的是「能装多少」 display becoming sharper and storage __(14)__ increasing：display sharper 谈显示 【选项】A) ability ✗ 侧重「会做的能力」 ability 强调主语「会做某事」的能力，多接 to do sth，与 storage 这种「容器属性」搭配不准。 B) capability ✗ 侧重潜在能力 C) capacity ✓ storage capacity 是术语 capacity 表「容量、容积」，storage capacity「存储容量」是 IT 领域常用术语；与下文 D) faculty ✗ 义偏「官能/院系」 【验证】代入后：display becoming sharper and storage capacity increasing，「显示更清晰、

in terms of 【线索】「像人一样按代际理解」 They were thought of, like people, __(15)__ generations, with the distance between generations much __(16)__：作者把计算机比作人，按「代际」这一概念来理解，本句内 【选项】A) by means of ✗ 表「凭借……方法」 by means of 意为「凭借、通过」，引出工具/手段，但 generations「代际」不是手段而是「理 B) in terms of ✓ in terms of 按某角度，精准对位 in terms of 表「按……来看、从……角度」，think of ... in terms of generations 即「按代际理 C) with regard to ✗ 表「关于」 with regard to 意为「关于、就……而言」，引出话题对象，而非「划分维度」，与本句「按代际 D) in line with ✗ 表「与……一致」 in line with 意为「与……一致、符合」，要求后接「标准/原则」，但 generations 不是标准，与 【验证】代入后：They were thought of, like people, in terms of generations, with the distance between generations much __(16)__，「按代际去看待计算机」与下一空所述

smaller 【线索】代际间隔越来越短 上一空 in terms of generations 已经把计算机的更新换代比作「代际」，本句 with the distance between generations much __(16)__ 自然描绘代际之间的「间隔」，而计算机 【选项】A) deeper ✗ deeper 修深度 deeper 表「更深」，描述纵深，但 distance 谈的是「间隔大小」，二者不是同一维度。 B) fewer ✗ fewer 修可数名词 fewer 只能修饰可数名词（fewer generations 才行），不能修饰 distance（不可数概念），语 C) nearer ✗ nearer 描述距离主体相对位置 nearer 表「更近」，多形容物体「靠得更近」，主语应是物体本身，而非 distance；distance nearer 搭配不地道。 D) smaller ✓ smaller 修 distance 最地道 smaller 表「更小」，distance much smaller「间隔小得多」是表示「代际间隔越来越短」的地 【验证】代入后：with the distance between generations much smaller，「代际间隔变小得多」 与上文 in terms of generations 的代际比喻浑然一体，呼应整段「计算机不断加速更新」

context 【线索】「我们生活其中的」=语境/环境 the __(17)__ within which we now live：定语从句明示「我们生活在其中」，说明这是一 个能容纳我们生活的「整体语境/环境」，与 information society 这一时代概念一致。 【选项】 A) context ✓ context 语境，与「身处其中」匹配 和 within which we now live 完全契合。 B) range ✗ range 偏「量幅/区间」 range 表「范围、幅度」，多用于具体量值的跨度（temperature range、price range），不指人 C) scope ✗ scope 表「范围/视野」 D) territory ✗ territory 指地理/领域 【验证】代入后：the term "information society" began to be widely used to describe the context within which we now live，「描述我们生活其中的时代语境」与全文「通信革命

influenced 【线索】革命对生活方方面面起作用 The communications revolution has __(18)__ both work and leisure and how we think and feel both about place and time：宾语横跨工作、休闲、时空感受，明显是 【选项】A) regarded ✗ regard 表「看作」 regarded 表「看作、认为」，多接 sb as sth，主语用「革命」去「看作」工作和闲暇不合理。 B) impressed ✗ impress 表「使印象深刻」 impressed 表「使……印象深刻」，宾语通常是人；impress work and leisure 不符合英语惯用。 C) influenced ✓ 影响工作与闲暇，精准对位 D) effected ✗ effect 表「使发生」 effected 作动词表「实现、使发生」，宾语通常是 change/reform，而非 work and leisure；此 【验证】代入后：The communications revolution has influenced both work and leisure and how we think and feel both about place and time，「通信革命已经影响了工作、休闲

controversial 【线索】权益对照「Benefits vs harmful outcomes」 本句紧随其后："Benefits" have been weighed __(20)__ "harmful" outcomes. And generalizations have proved difficult. 「益处」与「害处」被放在天平两端，且作者点明 【选项】A) competitive ✗ 竞争性偏商业义 B) controversial ✓ controversial 有争议，精准对位 controversial 表「有争议的、引起对立看法的」，与下文 Benefits vs harmful、 generalizations have proved difficult 完美呼应，是描述「对其经济、政治、社会、文化影响 C) distracting ✗ 「分散注意力」与观点无关 D) irrational ✗ irrational 表「非理性」 【验证】代入后：there have been controversial views about its economic, political, social and cultural implications，「对其经济、政治、社会、文化影响存在争议性观点」与紧接其后 的 Benefits vs harmful 对照、generalizations have proved difficult 的结论自洽。

against 【线索】「益处」与「害处」对立权衡 "Benefits" have been weighed __(20)__ "harmful" outcomes：benefits 与 harmful 【选项】A) above ✗ above 表位置高低 above 表「在……之上」，与 weigh 搭配会变成「比 harmful outcomes 更重要」，但作者并未 B) upon ✗ weigh upon 表「使忧虑」 upon 与 weigh 构成 weigh upon「使（人）忧虑/有压力」，主语应是负担，宾语是人，与「利 C) against ✓ weigh A against B 利弊权衡，精准对位 against 与 weigh 构成 weigh A against B「把 A 与 B 对比权衡」，正好处理 benefits 与 harmful outcomes 这一组利弊对照，意思自然、搭配地道。 D) with ✗ weigh with 不构成固定权衡义 with 与 weigh 没有「权衡利弊」的固定搭配，且 weigh with sb 多义为「对……有分量、被……重 视」，与本句宾语 harmful outcomes 搭不上。 【验证】代入后："Benefits" have been weighed against "harmful" outcomes. And generalizations have proved difficult.「益处和害处被权衡比较，难以一概而论」是结尾 OVERVIEW · 通读建境 drawn between the development of television in the 20th century and the diffusion of printing in the 15th and 16th centuries.），结尾点出对其影响存在分歧（there have been __(19)__ views about its economic, political, social and cultural implications）。 广播、电影、汽车、飞机（beginning with transport, the railway, and leading __(6)__ through the telegraph, the telephone, radio, and motion pictures __(7)__ the 20th century world of the motor car and the airplane.）。第二段聚焦计算机：以转折切入（It is generally recognized, __(9)__, that the introduction of the computer in the early 20th 并点出评价分歧（there have been __(19)__ views about its economic, political, social and cultural implications.）。逐空作答时必须依托这条递进脉络判逻辑、辨词义。 SENTENCE INSIGHTS · 句子精讲 7 As was discussed before, it was not until the 19th century that the newspaper became the dominant pre-electronic me...

sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: If you intend using humor in your talk to make people smile, you must know how to identify shared experiences and problems. Your humor must be relevant to the audience and should help to show them that you are one of them or that you understand their situation and are in sympathy with their point of view. Depending on whom you are addressing, the problems will be different. If you are talking to a group of managers, you may refer to the disorganized methods of their secretaries; alternatively if you are addressing secretaries, you may want to comment on their disorganized bosses. Here is an example, which I heard at a nurses' convention, of a story which works well because the audience all shared the same view of doctors. A man arrives in heaven and is being shown around by St. Peter. He sees wonderful accommodations, beautiful gardens, sunny weather, and so on. Everyone is very peaceful, polite and friendly until, waiting in a line for lunch, the new arrival is suddenly pushed aside by a man in a white coat, who rushes to the head of the line, grabs his food and stomps over to a table by himself. "Who is that?" the new arrival asked St. Peter. "Oh, that's God," came the reply, "but sometimes he thinks he's a doctor." If you are part of the group which you are addressing, you will be in a position to know the experiences and problems which are common to all of you and it'll be appropriate for you to make a passing remark about the inedible canteen food or the chairman's notorious bad taste in ties. With other audiences you mustn't attempt to cut in with humor as they will resent an outsider making disparaging remarks about their canteen or their chairman. You will be on safer ground if you stick to scapegoats like the Post Office or the telephone system. If you feel awkward being humorous, you must practice so that it becomes more natural. Include a few casual and apparently off-the-cuff remarks which you can deliver in a relaxed and unforced manner. Often it's the delivery which causes the audience to smile, so speak slowly and remember that a raised eyebrow or an unbelieving look may help to show that you are making a light-hearted remark. Look for the humor. It often comes from the unexpected. A twist on a familiar quote "If at first you don't succeed, give up" or a play on words or on a situation. Search for exaggeration and understatement. Look at your talk and pick out a few words or sentences which you can turn about and inject with humor.

Since the dawn of human ingenuity, people have devised ever more cunning tools to cope with work that is dangerous, boring, burdensome, or just plain nasty. That compulsion has resulted in robotics—the science of conferring various human capabilities on machines. And if scientists have yet to create the mechanical version of science fiction, they have begun to come close. As a result, the modern world is increasingly populated by intelligent gizmos whose presence we barely notice but whose universal existence has removed much human labor. Our factories hum to the rhythm of robot assembly arms. Our banking is done at automated teller terminals that thank us with mechanical politeness for the transaction. Our subway trains are controlled by tireless robot-drivers. And thanks to the continual miniaturization of electronics and micro-mechanics, there are already robot systems that can perform some kinds of brain and bone surgery with submillimeter accuracy—far greater precision than highly skilled physicians can achieve with their hands alone. But if robots are to reach the next stage of laborsaving utility, they will have to operate with less human supervision and be able to make at least a few decisions for themselves—goals that pose a real challenge. "While we know how to tell a robot to handle a specific error," says Dave Lavery, manager of a robotics program at NASA, "we can't yet give a robot enough 'common sense' to reliably interact with a dynamic world." Indeed the quest for true artificial intelligence has produced very mixed results. Despite a spell of initial optimism in the 1960s and 1970s when it appeared that transistor circuits and microprocessors might be able to copy the action of the human brain by the year 2010, researchers lately have begun to extend that forecast by decades if not centuries. What they found, in attempting to model thought, is that the human brain's roughly one hundred billion nerve cells are much more talented—and human perception far more complicated—than previously imagined. They have built robots that can recognize the error of a machine panel by a fraction of a millimeter in a controlled factory environment. But the human mind can glimpse a rapidly changing scene and immediately disregard the 98 percent that is irrelevant, instantaneously focusing on the monkey at the side of a winding forest road or the single suspicious face in a big crowd. The most advanced computer systems on Earth can't approach that kind of ability, and neuroscientists still don't know quite how we do it.

Could the bad old days of economic decline be about to return? Since OPEC agreed to supply-cuts in March, the price of crude oil has jumped to almost $26 a barrel, up from less than $10 last December. This near-tripling of oil prices calls up scary memories of the 1973 oil shock, when prices quadrupled, and 1979- 1980, when they also almost tripled. Both previous shocks resulted in double-digit inflation and global economic decline. So where are the headlines warning of gloom and doom this time? The oil price was given another push up this week when Iraq suspended oil exports. Strengthening economic growth, at the same time as winter grips the northern hemisphere, could push the price higher still in the short term. Yet there are good reasons to expect the economic consequences now to be less severe than in the 1970s. In most countries the cost of crude oil now accounts for a smaller share of the price of petrol than it did in the 1970s. In Europe, taxes account for up to four-fifths of the retail price, so even quite big changes in the price of crude have a more muted effect on pump prices than in the past. Rich economies are also less dependent on oil than they were, and so less sensitive to swings in the oil price. Energy conservation, a shift to other fuels and a decline in the importance of heavy, energy-intensive industries have reduced oil consumption. Software, consultancy and mobile telephones use far less oil than steel or car production. For each dollar of GDP (in constant prices) rich economies now use nearly 50% less oil than in 1973. The OECD estimates in its latest Economic Outlook that, if oil prices averaged $22 a barrel for a full year, compared with $13 in 1998, this would increase the oil import bill in rich economies by only 0.25-0.5% of GDP. That is less than one-quarter of the income loss in 1974 or 1980. On the other hand, oil-importing emerging economies—to which heavy industry has shifted—have become more energy-intensive, and so could be more seriously squeezed. One more reason not to lose sleep over the rise in oil prices is that, unlike the rises in the 1970s, it has not occurred against the background of general commodity-price inflation and global excess demand. A sizable portion of the world is only just emerging from economic decline. The Economist's commodity price index is broadly unchanging from a year ago. In 1973 commodity prices jumped by 70%, and in 1979 by almost 30%.

The Supreme Court's decisions on physician-assisted suicide carry important implications for how medicine seeks to relieve dying patients of pain and suffering. Although it ruled that there is no constitutional right to physician-assisted suicide, the Court in effect supported the medical principle of "double effect", a centuries-old moral principle holding that an action having two effects—a good one that is intended and a harmful one that is foreseen—is permissible if the actor intends only the good effect. Doctors have used that principle in recent years to justify using high doses of morphine to control terminally ill patients' pain, even though increasing dosages will eventually kill the patient. Nancy Dubler, director of Montefiore Medical Center, contends that the principle will shield doctors who "until now have very, very strongly insisted that they could not give patients sufficient medication to control their pain if that might hasten death". George Annas, chair of the health law department at Boston University, maintains that, as long as a doctor prescribes a drug for a legitimate medical purpose, the doctor has done nothing illegal even if the patient uses the drug to hasten death. "It's like surgery," he says. "We don't call those deaths homicides because the doctors didn't intend to kill their patients, although they risked their death. If you're a physician, you can risk your patient's suicide as long as you don't intend their suicide." On another level, many in the medical community acknowledge that the assisted-suicide debate has been fueled in part by the despair of patients for whom modern medicine has prolonged the physical agony of dying. Just three weeks before the Court's ruling on physician-assisted suicide, the National Academy of Science (NAS) released a two-volume report, Approaching Death: Improving Care at the End of Life. It identifies the undertreatment of pain and the aggressive use of "ineffectual and forced medical procedures that may prolong and even dishonor the period of dying" as the twin problems of end-of-life care. The profession is taking steps to require young doctors to train in hospices, to test knowledge of aggressive pain management therapies, to develop a Medicare billing code for hospital-based care, and to develop new standards for assessing and treating pain at the end of life. Annas says lawyers can play a key role in insisting that these well-meaning medical initiatives translate into better care. "Large numbers of physicians seem unconcerned with the pain their patients are needlessly and predictably suffering", to the extent that it constitutes "systematic patient abuse". He says medical licensing boards "must make it clear…that painful deaths are presumptively ones that are incompetently managed and should result in license suspension".

questions.question: George Annas would probably agree that doctors should be punished if they____. Part B Directions: Read the following text carefully and then translate the underlined segments into Chinese. Write your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. ( 10 points) Almost all our major problems involve human behavior, and they cannot be solved by physical and biological technology alone. What is needed is a technology of behavior, but we have been slow to develop the science from which such a technology might be drawn. (41)One difficulty is that almost all of what is called behavioral science continues to trace behavior to states of mind, feelings, traits of character, human nature, and so on. Physics and biology once followed similar practices and advanced only when they discarded them. (42)The behavioral sciences have been slow to change partly because the explanatory items often seem to be directly observed and partly because other kinds of explanations have been hard to find. The environment is obviously important, but its role has remained obscure. It does not push or pull, it selects, and this function is difficult to discover and analyze. (43)The role of natural selection in evolution was formulated only a little more than a hundred years ago, and the selective role of the environment in shaping and maintaining the behavior of the individual is only beginning to be recognized and studied. As the interaction between organism and environment has come to be understood, however, effects once assigned to states of mind, feelings, and traits are beginning to be traced to accessible conditions, and a technology of behavior may therefore become available. It will not solve our problems, however, until it replaces traditional prescientific views, and these are strongly entrenched. Freedom and dignity illustrate the difficulty. (44)They are the possessions of the autonomous(self- governing) man of traditional theory, and they are essential to practices in which a person is held responsible for his conduct and given credit for his achievements. A scientific analysis shifts both the responsibility and the achievement to the environment. It also raises questions concerning "values". Who will use a technology and to what ends? (45)Until these issues are resolved, a technology of behavior will continue to be rejected, and with it possibly the only way to solve our problems.
